question: When a patient presents after ingesting a strong acid (e.g., sulphuric acid), administering a dilute alkali (e.g., sodium bicarbonate) orally is an effective first-aid measure to neutralise the acid and reduce tissue injury.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. Alkali neutralisation is dangerous: it is exothermic (releases heat, worsening burns) and generates CO₂ gas (causing gastric distension and perforation risk). Give only water or milk for dilution; never attempt chemical neutralisation in acid ingestion.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Incorrect. Neutralisation with an alkali is CONTRAINDICATED. The exothermic acid–alkali reaction generates intense heat, deepening the burns. CO₂ gas produced causes acute gastric distension and risks perforation. Correct management: dilution with water or milk only.
